# Judith Chapter 1 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 14

---

## Disagreement 1 — Verse 1:1: Opening Structure

**EMET:** Renders as a single long sentence following Greek syntax: "In-the twelfth year... who reigned over-the Assyrians in Nineveh, the-great city, in-the days of Arphaxad, who was-reigning over-the Medes in Ecbatana —" (em-dash suspending the sentence).
**LOGOS:** Splits into two sentences at "In those days Arphaxad was ruling over the Medes in Ecbatana."
**PNEUMA:** Opens with "This is the story of what happened" — a narrative frame not present in the Greek.
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS structure adopted. The Greek opening is characteristically periodic but English benefits from the clarifying break. PNEUMA's narrative frame is a significant addition without Greek warrant; rejected.

---

## Disagreement 2 — Verse 1:1: "reigned over the Assyrians"

**EMET/LOGOS:** "ruled/reigned over the Assyrians in Nineveh."
**PNEUMA:** "He called himself king of the Assyrians" — adds interpretive commentary about the historical fiction.
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS phrasing adopted. The author's deliberate anachronism (Nebuchadnezzar was Babylonian, not Assyrian) is historically significant but should not be flagged by the translation itself; a footnote is the appropriate vehicle.

---

## Disagreement 3 — Verse 1:2: Wall dimensions — "hewn stones"

**EMET:** "walls of-hewn-stones, three cubits in-breadth and six cubits in-length."
**LOGOS:** "walls of hewn stones three cubits thick and six cubits long."
**PNEUMA:** "massive hewn stones, each three cubits thick and six cubits long."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS phrasing. "Thick and long" is clearer than "breadth and length" for construction context. PNEUMA's "massive" adds an evaluative term absent in the Greek.

---

## Disagreement 4 — Verse 1:4: Purpose clause

**EMET:** "for-the going-out of-his armies of-power and for-the marshaling of his infantry."
**LOGOS:** "to allow the passage of his mighty armies and the marshaling of his infantry."
**PNEUMA:** "wide enough to pour out his armies in battle formation."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "To allow the passage" is natural English. PNEUMA's "pour out" is vivid but loses the two-part structure (armies + infantry) that the Greek preserves.

---

## Disagreement 5 — Verse 1:6: "there-met to him" (συνήντησαν)

**EMET:** "there-met to him all-the ones dwelling [in] the-hill-country."
**LOGOS:** "All the inhabitants of the hill country came to meet him."
**PNEUMA:** "Arphaxad was not alone. The hill tribes rallied to him."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Came to meet him" captures the Greek idiom well. PNEUMA's paragraph break and "was not alone" are dramatic additions.

---

## Disagreement 6 — Verse 1:6: "sons of Cheloud"

**EMET/LOGOS/PNEUMA:** All preserve "sons of Cheloud" as a proper name.
**PNEUMA:** Writes "Scores of nations under the sons of Cheloud" adding "scores of."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Many peoples" (LOGOS) preferred over PNEUMA's quantifying addition. Greek has πολλὰ ἔθνη = "many nations/peoples."

---

## Disagreement 7 — Verse 1:7: List formatting

**EMET:** Single long hyphenated compound sentence with all nations listed.
**LOGOS:** Single sentence with em-dash introducing the list.
**PNEUMA:** Breaks into three separate sentences with "He summoned" introducing subsections.
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS structure. The Greek uses one extended sentence; PNEUMA's fragmentation loses the sense of imperial breadth conveyed by the catalogue.

---

## Disagreement 8 — Verse 1:11: "he was to them as a man of one"

**EMET:** "for he-was to them as a man of one" — literal rendering of ὡς ἀνὴρ εἷς.
**LOGOS:** "He seemed to them like a single man of no account."
**PNEUMA:** "He was just one man among many, nothing special."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The Greek idiom conveys contempt through the image of "just one man" — LOGOS's "of no account" is a reasonable gloss. EMET's "man of one" is too opaque. PNEUMA's "nothing special" is colloquial.

---

## Disagreement 9 — Verse 1:11: "empty-handed, in disgrace"

**EMET:** "empty-handed, in-disgrace."
**LOGOS:** "empty-handed and in disgrace."
**PNEUMA:** "empty-handed and humiliated."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "In disgrace" is more precise to the Greek κενοὺς ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ.

---

## Disagreement 10 — Verse 1:12: Oath formula

**EMET:** "he-swore by-his throne and by-his kingdom."
**LOGOS/PNEUMA:** "he swore by his throne and his kingdom."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS/PNEUMA (drop second "by" as natural English). Negligible.

---

## Disagreement 11 — Verse 1:12: Scope of vengeance

**EMET:** "to-kill with-the sword also all-the ones dwelling in-the land of Moab and the-sons of Ammon and all-[those-of] Judea."
**LOGOS:** "putting to the sword all who dwelt in the land of Moab and the Ammonites and all Judea."
**PNEUMA:** "Moab, Ammon, Judea, Egypt — the sword." (Dramatic list, loses relative clause structure.)
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. Preserves the list while rendering naturally. PNEUMA's telegraphic style loses the formal legal/oath quality of the threat.

---

## Disagreement 12 — Verse 1:13: "prevailed in his battle"

**EMET:** "he-prevailed in-his battle."
**LOGOS:** "prevailed in the battle."
**PNEUMA:** "crushed him."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The Greek ἐκράτησεν ἐν τῇ παρατάξει αὐτοῦ is "prevailed in his battle formation/engagement." PNEUMA loses the military technical term.

---

## Disagreement 13 — Verse 1:15: Killing of Arphaxad

**EMET:** "he-struck him down with his spears, and he-utterly-destroyed him until that-day."
**LOGOS:** "ran him through with his spears, and utterly destroyed him on that day."
**PNEUMA:** "killed him with his own spear." (Singular; adds "his own.")
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The Greek has plural "spears" (ἀκοντίοις). "Ran him through" is vivid and accurate. PNEUMA's singular "spear" and "his own" are additions not in the text.

---

## Disagreement 14 — Verse 1:16: Celebration period

**EMET:** "there he-rested-at-ease, he and his force, for a hundred-and-twenty days."
**LOGOS:** "there he rested and feasted, he and his army, for one hundred and twenty days."
**PNEUMA:** "he and his army spent the next four months in celebration." (Converts to months; adds "the next.")
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. Days should be preserved as days — the specific number (120) is a narrative detail. PNEUMA's conversion to "four months" is interpretively accurate but loses the precision of the original.
